# The Peculiar Grace of Getting Lost

There's something about being genuinely lost that strips away the modern world's comfortable pretenses. Not lost in an abstract sense—not lost in purpose or direction, though those are their own particular hells—but lost in the most literal, geographical way. You've turned onto a road that looked right, or followed directions that were confidently given but apparently incorrect, and now you cannot quite figure out where you are. The maps on your phone might not be helping. The sun is setting. You've been driving in circles for twenty minutes.

I've been thinking about this a lot lately, particularly after a friend mentioned that her teenage daughter had never been properly lost. Never gone out with uncertain directions, never had to ask a stranger for help, never felt that particular blend of anxiety and adventure that comes from not knowing where you are. The GPS has eliminated something from the human experience, and I'm not entirely sure what we've gained in return.

When I was young, being lost was a rite of passage. My parents would let me wander the neighborhood with the vague instruction to "be home by dark," and I would inevitably end up several blocks further than intended, squinting at street signs and trying to reconstruct the turns I'd made. There was genuine fear in it, yes—what if I couldn't find my way back? What if I had to ask a stranger? What if my mother worried?—but there was also freedom. I was navigating the world by my own judgment and memory. The world felt larger, less predetermined.

I think there's something about lostness that modern life is actively designed to prevent, and I'm not sure that's entirely good.

Consider the psychology of it. When you're lost, you must become observant. You notice which way the sun is moving, whether the streets are widening or narrowing, whether you recognize landmarks. You become attuned to your environment in a way that GPS prevents. When you're following turn-by-turn directions, you're in a kind of cognitive autopilot—turn right at the next light, continue 2.3 miles, turn left. The route is disembodied, abstract. You could be anywhere, following any set of instructions. But when you're lost, the place becomes real. You notice that there's a distinctive red brick building on this corner, that the street slopes downward to your left, that you've definitely seen this church before, wasn't it three blocks back?

There's also something about getting lost that forces a kind of radical acceptance. You cannot worry your way to knowing where you are. You cannot think yourself unlost. You must actually do something—turn around, ask for directions, look at a physical map, try a different route. There's a problem and a required action. It's almost meditative in its clarity, once you accept that you are, in fact, lost.

I wonder if this is part of why so many people find hiking or backpacking valuable. You go out deliberately to get away from the systems that keep you located—cellular data, GPS, the constant pinpointing that modern technology allows. And many people find this deeply restorative. They come back transformed by the experience of not knowing, for a time, exactly where they are. The uncertainty becomes freedom.

Of course, there's a dark side to this romanticism. Getting lost can be genuinely dangerous. A woman lost in the wrong part of town at night faces different risks than a man. A child lost for real—not playing lost, but truly separated from their parents—might be experiencing genuine terror. There's a reason GPS technology has been celebrated: it makes travel safer, allows real-time location sharing, prevents people from disappearing. The parent who can track their teenager's location via their phone has legitimate reasons for that parental surveillance. The elderly person with dementia can be found if they wander.

But I think we've overcorrected. We've designed a world where uncertainty is treated as a problem to be solved, rather than a condition to be navigated. And I'm not sure we're better for it.

There's a concept in psychology called "situational awareness," and it's something that's been studied extensively in emergency response and self-defense contexts. People who are paying attention to their surroundings—noticing exits, recognizing patterns, reading social cues—tend to respond better to unexpected situations. But this kind of awareness requires a certain amount of attention, the kind that gets atrophied when you're following exact directions on a screen.

I'm not suggesting we throw away our phones or go back to paper maps exclusively. That would be performative and unrealistic. But I think there's something worth preserving about the experience of not knowing, of having to navigate by observation and intuition rather than instruction.

My grandfather had an interesting approach to this. He would deliberately take wrong turns when driving somewhere new, just to force himself to figure out how to get back. He wanted to build a mental map of the area, and he knew that learning required some failure, some disorientation. He would end up in random neighborhoods, dead ends, confusing intersections, and he would find his way back by logic and attention. It made him an unusually good driver, I think—intuitive about how cities were laid out, comfortable in unfamiliar places.

There's also something about being lost that's good for humility. When everything is directing you, when you have perfect information, there's a tendency to move through the world as though everything should conform to your expectations. You become entitled to certainty. But when you're lost, you're reminded that the world is larger than your knowledge of it, more complex than your maps suggest. You're reminded that you don't actually know as much as you thought you did.

I've noticed this in other domains too. People who've done a lot of reading in physical libraries have a different relationship with knowledge than people who've only searched online. Yes, online searching is faster and more efficient. You can find exactly what you're looking for in seconds. But there's something lost in that efficiency. When you had to browse the stacks, you encountered books you weren't looking for. You'd be searching for something about medieval history and stumble upon a fascinating book about textile production, which led you to another book about trade routes, which connected to something else entirely. These unexpected connections shaped how you thought. But they weren't efficient.

Efficiency is a genuine good in many contexts, but it's become our primary value, and I'm not sure that's right.

There's also something to be said about the emotional texture of being lost. Yes, there's anxiety, particularly in the first moments of realization. But there can also be a kind of adventure, a openness to whatever happens. You might stumble upon a wonderful restaurant you never would have found otherwise. You might have an interesting conversation with someone who gives you directions. You might discover a beautiful street or a view you wouldn't have seen. The lostness becomes generative, productive of experience in a way that arriving efficiently at your destination might not be.

I think modern life, for many of us, has become too predictable. We know where we're going before we go there—we've looked it up online, read reviews, seen pictures. We know what to order before we arrive at the restaurant. Our social feeds are algorithmically curated to show us more of what we already like. The surprises have been minimized, engineered out of the system. And while this reduces certain kinds of friction, it also reduces the richness of engagement with the world.

Sometimes I deliberately take long routes when I'm driving, or wander into neighborhoods I don't know. It's a small rebellion against the optimization of existence. And inevitably, I find something I wouldn't have found otherwise. Sometimes it's just a pretty street corner. Sometimes it's a good bookstore or a interesting mural. Sometimes it's the simple experience of not knowing where I am, and then figuring it out.

My friend's daughter, the one who's never been properly lost, is starting to drive. I wonder what her experience of the world will be like if she's always being directed, always knowing where she is. I wonder if she'll develop the same intuitive sense of place that my grandfather had. I wonder if she'll ever experience that peculiar combination of anxiety and freedom that comes from genuine disorientation.

I think we should let people get lost more often. Obviously, not dangerously, not in ways that cause real harm. But in controlled ways, deliberately. Let them navigate by observation. Let them ask strangers for directions. Let them experience the world as larger and less knowable than their maps suggest.

There's a kind of wisdom that only comes from lostness, from realizing that the world doesn't conform to your expectations and plans. And we need that wisdom now, I think, when so much of life is algorithmically predicted, when certainty is sold to us as a premium product, when the unknown has been rebranded as a problem to be solved rather than a condition to be experienced.

Getting lost, real lost, forces you to slow down. It forces you to pay attention. It forces you to accept that you don't know everything, that your plans can be disrupted, that the world is still larger than your knowledge of it. And maybe, in a world that's trying very hard to make everything predictable and controllable, that's exactly the grace we need most.
